title: Air-Fluid Exchange (AFX): A Core Vitreoretinal Maneuver
summary: Air-fluid exchange (AFX) is a fundamental, multi-purpose technique in vitreoretinal surgery, crucial for achieving precise retinal reattachment, removing subretinal fluid, and preparing the eye for long-term tamponade. This infographic delves into the principles, techniques, indications, and management considerations of AFX, providing a comprehensive guide for ophthalmology residents and fellows.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Air-fluid exchange (AFX) is a critical intraoperative maneuver in pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) where intraocular fluid (vitreous substitute, balanced salt solution - BSS) is actively removed from the vitreous cavity and replaced with air. This process serves multiple purposes, primarily to facilitate retinal reattachment, allow drainage of subretinal fluid (SRF) through a retinotomy, and prepare the eye for instillation of a long-term tamponade agent (e.g., gas, silicone oil).

sections.title: 2. Principles & Mechanism
sections.content: AFX leverages surface tension to flatten the retina. As air replaces fluid, the air-fluid interface exerts a flattening force on the retina, pushing subretinal fluid anteriorly and encouraging its drainage through a peripheral retinotomy or retinal break. This creates a dry, stable retinal surface essential for laser photocoagulation (endolaser) and subsequent tamponade. Automated vitrectomy systems precisely control infusion pressure and aspiration to maintain globe stability and prevent iatrogenic damage.

sections.title: 4. Pre-operative Considerations
content: Thorough retinal drawing: Map all breaks, detachments, PVR membranes.
Assess lens status: Phakic vs. pseudophakic (cataract progression risk with long-term tamponade).
Patient education: Post-operative positioning, visual prognosis, need for tamponade.
Anesthesia: Local (peribulbar/retrobulbar) vs. General.

sections.title: 6. Step-by-Step Air-Fluid Exchange Process
content: **Step 1: Complete Vitrectomy** - Ensure all vitreous traction is relieved, membranes peeled, and retinal breaks are identified.
**Step 2: PFCL Instillation (Optional)** - For complex RRDs (e.g., GRT, PVR), PFCL is infused to flatten the retina from posterior to anterior, displacing SRF.
**Step 3: Initiate AFX** - Switch infusion from BSS to air. The infusion cannula (or chandelier) delivers air into the vitreous cavity.

**Step 4: Fluid Extrusion** - An extrusion cannula (often a soft-tip) is placed over the retinal break (or a created retinotomy) to actively aspirate subretinal fluid and intraocular BSS. The air-fluid interface advances posteriorly, pushing SRF out.

**Step 5: Complete Fluid Removal** - Meticulously remove all fluid, ensuring the retina is completely dry and flattened, especially around breaks. Pay attention to fluid behind the iris, in the ciliary sulcus, and under the lens/IOL.
**Step 6: Endolaser Photocoagulation** - Apply laser around all retinal breaks and along the ora serrata (if indicated) to create a chorioretinal adhesion.
**Step 7: Tamponade Agent Instillation** - Exchange air for the chosen long-term tamponade agent (e.g., SF6, C2F6, C3F8 gas, or silicone oil).

sections.title: 8. Complications of AFX & Tamponade
content: **Iatrogenic Retinal Break/Hole:** Due to mechanical trauma from extrusion cannula or excessive suction.
**Subretinal Air/Gas:** If extrusion cannula slips into subretinal space or excessive pressure forces air under retina.
**Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE) Damage:** From aggressive aspiration of SRF, especially at the edge of a break.
**Hypotony/Hypertony:** Poor control of infusion pressure during AFX.
**Cataract Progression:** Especially in phakic eyes with gas/oil tamponade.
**Increased Intraocular Pressure (IOP):** Post-operative, particularly with expanding gas bubbles or silicone oil emulsification/pupillary block.
**Corneal Edema/Decompensation:** Prolonged contact with air/gas, especially in compromised corneas.
**Silicone Oil Emulsification:** Leading to glaucoma, keratopathy, or secondary detachment.
**Endophthalmitis:** As with any intraocular surgery.

sections.title: 9. Post-operative Management & Patient Guidance
sections.content: Post-AFX management is dictated by the tamponade agent used. Patients with gas tamponade require strict posturing (e.g., face-down for macular holes, specific side for superior breaks) to ensure optimal gas-retina contact. They must avoid flying and high altitudes due to gas expansion. Silicone oil patients do not require specific posturing but may need future oil removal surgery. Topical antibiotics, steroids, and cycloplegics are routinely prescribed. IOP monitoring is crucial, especially in the early post-operative period.

sections.title: 10. Key Clinical Pearls
content: **Slow & Steady:** AFX should be performed slowly and methodically to prevent iatrogenic breaks and ensure complete fluid removal.
**Gravity is Your Friend:** Position the eye so that the break is the most dependent point for efficient SRF drainage.
**Peripheral Extrusion:** Always extrude fluid over a retinal break or a created retinotomy, not directly on healthy retina.
**"Dry" Retina:** Aim for a completely dry retinal surface before performing endolaser; residual fluid compromises laser adhesion.
**Watch the Lens:** In phakic eyes, avoid prolonged air contact with the posterior lens capsule to minimize cataract formation.

sections.title: 11. Pediatric Considerations for AFX
sections.content: AFX in pediatric vitrectomy (e.g., ROP-related detachments, persistent fetal vasculature) requires special attention. Pediatric eyes are smaller, sclera is more elastic, and lens is highly susceptible to cataract formation. Use smaller gauge instruments (25G/27G), lower infusion pressures, and minimize air exposure to the lens. General anesthesia is mandatory. Long-term gas tamponade can be challenging due to non-compliance with posturing, making silicone oil a frequent choice despite its need for a second surgery.

sections.title: 12. Recent Advances & Techniques
content: **Automated AFX Systems:** Integration into modern vitrectomy machines for precise control of air pressure and flow rates, reducing manual error.
**Heated Air:** Some systems offer heated air to maintain intraocular temperature, theoretically reducing corneal stress and facilitating better visualization.

**Denser Tamponade Agents:** Development of heavy silicone oils (e.g., Densiron 68, Oxane HD) for complex inferior retinal detachments where conventional silicone oil may fail to provide adequate tamponade.
**Vitrectomy Port Design:** Improved cannula designs for smoother entry and reduced tissue drag, minimizing iatrogenic trauma during instrument exchanges.
